entities.label: 10 U.S.C. Sec. 119 - Special access programs: congressional oversight
entities.sub: Statute; the entire congressional reporting regime for DoD special access programs
entities.desc: Section 119 of title 10 is the only statute that tells the Secretary of Defense what he must tell Congress about special access programs, and it is therefore the exact place to look for how a program escapes oversight. It was added by section 1132(a)(1) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1988 and 1989, Public Law 100-180, signed 4 December 1987, and amended five times since (Pub. L. 101-510 in 1990, Pub. L. 104-106 in 1996, Pub. L. 106-65 in 1999, Pub. L. 107-107 in 2001). The architecture is four affirmative duties and one hole. Subsection (a)(1) requires the Secretary, 'not later than March 1 of each year', to submit to the defense committees 'a report on special access programs' setting forth the total amount requested for DoD SAPs in the President's budget and, for each program, a brief description, major milestones, actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and estimated cost for the current year, the budget year and the four succeeding years. Subsection (b)(1) requires, 'not later than February 1 of each year', notice of the designation of each 'new special access program' and 'justification for such designation', with the current total program cost estimate and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program'. Subsection (c) requires a report at least 14 days before any planned change in the classification of a SAP or any declassification and public release, with an exceptional-circumstances escape hatch. Subsection (d) requires prompt notice of any modification or termination of the policy and criteria used to designate programs as SAPs. Subsection (f) provides that 'A special access program may not be initiated until - (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' Subsection (g) defines 'defense committees' as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of both chambers plus the defense subcommittees of both Appropriations Committees. Then subsection (e) removes all of it. Nothing in section 119 defines 'special access program', creates a penalty for non-reporting, or gives any committee an enforcement remedy. The duty runs to the Secretary of Defense personally, which means a program concealed from the Secretary of Defense - which is what David Grusch and others allege - produces no statutory violation at all by anyone the statute names.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1): 'Not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs.'

10 U.S.C. 119(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated until - (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.'
10 U.S.C. 119(b)(3) defines 'new special access program' as 'a special access program that has not previously been covered in a notice and justification under this subsection.'
Section 119 was added by Public Law 100-180, div. A, title XI, sec. 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987, 101 Stat. 1151.
Section 119 contains no definition of 'special access program', no penalty provision, and no enforcement remedy for a committee that is not notified.

claims.text: Because every duty in section 119 is imposed on 'the Secretary of Defense', a program deliberately concealed from the Secretary of Defense generates no identifiable statutory violation by any named official. Reasoning: the statute has one obligor and no strict-liability provision reaching subordinate program managers or contractors.

entities.label: 10 U.S.C. Sec. 119(e) - the SAP reporting waiver
entities.sub: Statutory provision; the lawful mechanism by which a program disappears from the congressional record
entities.desc: Subsection (e) is the hinge of this entire board. In two paragraphs it converts the full committee reporting regime of section 119 into a briefing for a handful of individuals. Paragraph (1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' Paragraph (2): 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Four features matter. First, the waiver is unilateral - no committee concurrence, no ISOO review, no judicial test; the sole standard is the Secretary's own determination. Second, the waiver reaches subsections (a), (b) and (c) - the annual report, the new-program notice and the declassification notice - but not subsection (f), so the 30-day pre-initiation notice to the committees survives on paper. Third, the information does not vanish: it goes to named leaders, which is why programs run under a section 119(e) waiver are called 'waived' programs and are informally said to be briefed to a 'Gang of Eight'. Fourth, and decisively, section 119(e) contains no audit trail requirement - no register of waivers exercised, no annual accounting of how many waivers are outstanding, no requirement that the waived program appear anywhere in an unclassified count. The number of waived DoD special access programs currently in existence has never been published.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2): the Secretary 'shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'
The waiver authority extends only to subsections (a), (b) and (c); the 30-day pre-initiation notice requirement of subsection (f) is not waivable on the face of the statute.
Section 119(e) imposes no requirement to maintain, publish or report a register of waivers exercised.

Read literally, 119(g) names six bodies - Senate Armed Services, Senate Appropriations, the Defense Subcommittee of Senate Appropriations, and the three House counterparts - so 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' is up to twelve members, not eight. The conventional 'Gang of Eight' framing for defense waived programs counts only the four parent committees. Reasoning: statutory text versus practice convention.

entities.label: The defense committees (10 U.S.C. 119(g))
entities.sub: Statutorily defined set of six congressional bodies; the intended recipients of the SAP record
entities.desc: Section 119(g) defines the term that governs who gets told. As amended by Public Law 104-106 in 1996, Public Law 106-65 in 1999 and Public Law 107-107 in 2001, it means '(1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' The definition is the reason the SAP record is structurally invisible to the rest of Congress: the House Oversight Committee, which has held every public UAP hearing since 26 July 2023, is not a defense committee and has no statutory entitlement to the section 119 reports. Neither are the intelligence committees; they sit under a wholly separate regime in title 50. Before 1996 the definition was broader in one respect and narrower in another - the prior text referred simply to 'the Committees on Armed Services and Appropriations of the Senate and House' and 'the Defense Subcommittees of the Committees on Appropriations'. The 1996 amendment made the enumeration explicit. The practical consequence for this board: a member of Congress who is not on one of these six bodies and not on an intelligence committee has no lawful route to a SAP list at all, which is precisely the wall the 2023-2026 UAP oversight effort has repeatedly hit.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of the Senate and House plus the Defense Subcommittee of Senate Appropriations and the Subcommittee on Defense of House Appropriations - six bodies.

Public Law 107-107 (28 December 2001) substituted 'Subcommittee on Defense' for 'National Security Subcommittee' in 119(g)(2); Public Law 106-65 (1999) substituted 'Committee on Armed Services' for 'Committee on National Security'.
The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is not a defense committee within the meaning of 10 U.S.C. 119(g) and receives no report under that section.

entities.label: Public Law 100-180, sec. 1132 - creation of SAP congressional oversight
entities.sub: FY1988-89 NDAA provision that first imposed any reporting duty on DoD special access programs
entities.desc: Until 4 December 1987 there was no statute at all requiring the Department of Defense to tell Congress that a special access program existed. Section 1132(a)(1) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1988 and 1989 added section 119 to title 10, at 101 Stat. 1151. The date is load-bearing for this board's chronology: every alleged legacy recovery and reverse-engineering activity from the 1940s through 1987 - the entire period covering Roswell, Project SIGN, Project BLUE BOOK's termination, the 1970s nuclear-site overflights and the origins of the alleged retrieval effort - ran in a legal environment in which no SAP reporting obligation to Congress existed whatsoever. A program stood up before December 1987 and never re-baselined was never a 'new special access program' within the meaning of subsection (b)(3), because that term is defined as one 'that has not previously been covered in a notice and justification under this subsection' - a definition that, on its face, does not reach back before the subsection existed.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119 was 'Added Pub. L. 100-180, div. A, title XI, sec. 1132(a)(1), Dec. 4, 1987, 101 Stat. 1151'.

A DoD special access program initiated before 4 December 1987 and never re-designated would fall outside the subsection (b) 'new special access program' notice regime and outside the subsection (f) 30-day pre-initiation notice, both of which operate prospectively. Reasoning: neither provision contains retroactive language, and (b)(3) defines the trigger by reference to prior notice under a subsection that did not exist.

entities.label: Executive Order 13526, Classified National Security Information
entities.sub: Presidential order, 29 December 2009; the sole source of authority to create a special access program
entities.desc: Executive Order 13526, signed by President Obama on 29 December 2009 and still the operative classification order in August 2026, is where special access programs actually come from. Section 4.3 provides that 'Unless otherwise authorized by the President, only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program' - and that for programs pertaining to intelligence activities, sources or methods, 'this function shall be exercised by the Director of National Intelligence'. The order requires that a SAP be created only on a specific finding that the vulnerability of, or threat to, the information is exceptional and that normal classification and safeguarding criteria are insufficient; that the number of programs be kept 'at an absolute minimum'; that each program be reviewed annually to determine whether it continues to meet the criteria; and, critically, that special access programs 'shall be subject to the oversight program established under section 5.4(d)' with the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office 'afforded access to these programs, consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President'. Two structural facts follow. First, SAP creation authority is a delegated executive power that Congress has never legislated over, so the six creating officials can stand a program up without any statutory basis and 10 U.S.C. 119 only tells them what to report afterward. Second, the ISOO access right in section 4.3 is qualified by 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President' - a clause that has been read to permit the President to withhold ISOO access to specific programs, which is the single most important limitation on independent oversight of the SAP enterprise.

claims.text: E.O. 13526 sec. 4.3(a): 'Unless otherwise authorized by the President, only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program.'

E.O. 13526 sec. 4.3(a) provides that for programs pertaining to intelligence activities, including special activities, or intelligence sources or methods, this function shall be exercised by the Director of National Intelligence.

E.O. 13526 sec. 4.3(b) requires that special access programs be subject to the oversight program established under section 5.4(d) and that the Director of ISOO be afforded access to these programs, 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President'.

E.O. 13526 sec. 4.3 requires agency heads to keep the number of special access programs at an absolute minimum and to review each program annually to determine whether it continues to meet the criteria for creation.

The qualifier 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President' in section 4.3(b) makes ISOO's access to any given SAP defeasible by presidential direction, so ISOO cannot warrant that it has seen the full SAP inventory. Reasoning: the access right is expressly conditioned rather than absolute.

entities.label: Executive Order 12829, National Industrial Security Program
entities.sub: Presidential order, 6 January 1993; creates the NISP and the Cognizant Security Agency structure
entities.desc: Executive Order 12829 established the National Industrial Security Program to provide a single, government-wide industrial security regime for contractors handling classified information. Section 201 of the order directs the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with all affected agencies and with the concurrence of the Secretary of Energy, the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Homeland Security, to issue and maintain the NISP Operating Manual - the document now codified as 32 CFR Part 117. The order is the ancestor of the carve-out: because it designates the Secretary of Defense as the issuing authority for the manual and DCSA (formerly the Defense Security Service) as the DoD Cognizant Security Office, it also creates the office from which a special access program can be exempted. Its practical importance to this board is that the NISP is the only routine, recurring, adversarial physical inspection of a contractor facility holding classified material. Where the NISP applies, a government inspector who is not part of the program walks the facility. Where it has been carved out, no such person exists.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.6(a)(1) records that the USD(I&S) 'Carries out the direction in section 201 of E.O. 12829 that the Secretary of Defense issue and maintain this rule and changes to it', in consultation with affected agencies and with the concurrence of the Secretary of Energy, the Chairman of the NRC, the DNI, and the Secretary of Homeland Security.

entities.label: DoD Directive 5205.07, Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (1 July 2010, Change 1 31 Aug 2018)
entities.sub: Superseded DoD directive; the version that defined acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived SAPs and created the SAPOC
entities.desc: This is the version of DoD's SAP charter that governed for the entire period covered by the Elizondo, Grusch and Kirkpatrick record, and it is the version cross-referenced by the NISPOM rule at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3). It reissued the 5 January 2006 directive, established the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, established the DoD SAP Central Office under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, and set out in plain language the three things this board most needs documented. First, the taxonomy: its glossary defines an acknowledged SAP as one 'whose existence is acknowledged but its specific details (technologies, materials, techniques, etc.) are classified'; an unacknowledged SAP as one 'having protective controls ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information'; and a waived SAP as 'A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting in accordance with Reference (c) following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls.' Reference (c) is section 119 of title 10. Second, the congressional access rule: members of the defense and intelligence committees are authorised access to DoD SAPs 'except for waived programs', and for waived SAPs 'only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors' are authorised access unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise. Third, the custody rule: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody. No copies shall be stored outside DoD repositories or control without the approval of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' A committee briefed on a waived program is not permitted to keep the paper.

entities.label: DoD Instruction 5205.11, Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs
entities.sub: 6 February 2013, Change 1 31 August 2018; the operating procedure for standing up a SAP and carving it out
entities.desc: DoDI 5205.11 is the single most useful public document on this board, because it does not merely define the mechanism - it walks through it, with a worked example and a timeline. Enclosure 6 sets out the prospective SAP (PSAP) approval sequence in days from establishment: SSWG review by P+14, draft security classification guide by P+45, approval package to the Senior Review Group by P+90, SRG convenes at P+105, final package to the SAPOC at P+130, SAPOC convenes at P+150, Deputy Secretary of Defense decision and congressional notification or termination at P+180, and 'End of 30-day period without Congressional decision' at P+210. The last line is the statutory clock of 10 U.S.C. 119(f) reduced to a checkbox: Congress is not asked to approve anything, it is notified, and after thirty days of silence the program starts. Appendix 2 to Enclosure 6 is the SAP Approval Package Checklist, whose item 2 requires that 'If unacknowledged and reporting requirements are to be waived, attach justification to waive the requirements of Volumes 2A and 2B of DoD 7000.14-R' - the Financial Management Regulation - and whose item 11.d requires a 'Contract strategy (carve-out justification if applicable)'. Appendix 3 is an unclassified sample Action Memo to the Deputy Secretary of Defense recommending establishment of a fictional unacknowledged operations and support SAP nicknamed GREEN TREE, in which the Director of DoD SAPCO writes: 'The Defense Security Service will be carved out from its normal industrial security oversight responsibilities' and recommends 'that you approve GTE as an unacknowledged SAP and authorize carve-out status and the mandatory administration of CI polygraphs'. Enclosure 7 then requires that each SAP record file contain 'Written approval by SecDef or DepSecDef of carve-out status when DSS is relieved of industrial security oversight responsibilities' and 'The identification of SAP facilities ... that have been carved-out based upon this authority'. Those two records are the FOIA target that would settle the question of how many carved-out facilities exist.

An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.'

DoDI 5205.11 para 5.d requires every DoD SAP to be assigned an unclassified nickname generated under CJCSM 3150.29D, and provides that 'Unclassified nicknames will be used in the annual SAP report to Congress.'

DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 2 requires the Director, DoD SAPCO to establish 'policies and applicable procedures to satisfy reporting requirements for DSS carve-outs' and to provide 'DSS confirmation of SAP facilities where the DSS has been carved out of security oversight functions.'

Because the annual SAP report to Congress uses only unclassified nicknames, a member reading the list sees a word, not a mission. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 para 5.d expressly directs nickname use in the annual report and leaves the codeword optional and classified.

entities.label: DoD Directive 5205.07, Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (12 September 2024)
entities.sub: Current DoD SAP charter; reissued under the 2023 SAP Enterprise Reform memorandum, and it deletes the old taxonomy
entities.desc: The current directive, effective 12 September 2024, cancels the 1 July 2010 version as amended and incorporates the Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum 'Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform' of 11 July 2023. Two changes matter for this board. First, the governance structure is retained and strengthened: the SAPOC remains 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise for governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs', chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense, with the Director of DoD SAPCO as Executive Secretary of the SAPOC and the SRG and Chair of the SSWG, reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is stated to be 'by exception' and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. Second, and much more significant, the 2024 directive replaces the acknowledged / unacknowledged / waived taxonomy with two new categories - 'Joint Force Integration SAP', defined as 'A SAP intended for greater integration and sharing across the Joint Force and the broader SAP community', and 'Strategic Enabler SAP', defined as 'A SAP protecting capabilities or information that enable strategic competition and warrant more limited and restrictive sharing'. The words acknowledged, unacknowledged, waived and carve-out do not appear in its definitions section. This does not repeal 10 U.S.C. 119(e), which continues to authorise the reporting waiver, and it does not repeal 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), which continues to authorise the carve-out and still cites this very directive by number. The effect is that the two mechanisms most relevant to a concealed program survive in statute and in the Code of Federal Regulations while ceasing to be defined in the Department's own public charter - the terminology has been removed from the shop window without being removed from the shop. The directive also carries forward the congressional-contact reporting rule: 'All personnel accessed to DoD SAPs will notify the Director, DoD SAPCO ... when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress.'

entities.label: DoD Manual 5205.07 Volume 1, SAP Security Manual: General Procedures
entities.sub: 18 June 2015, Change 1 12 February 2018; the manual that defines carve-out and states what DSS stops doing
entities.desc: Volume 1 of the four-volume DoD SAP Security Manual assigns responsibilities and describes the general procedures for the administration of DoD SAP security, implementing the policy of DoDI 5205.11, and it incorporates and cancels the Revision 1 Department of Defense Overprint to the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual Supplement. Its Enclosure 2 contains the operative statement of what a carve-out removes. The Director, DSS - the office now called the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency - administers the NISP and issues facility clearances for defense contractors 'to include contractors performing on DoD SAPs'; but then, 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense', the Director performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations, authorises classified contractor SAP information systems and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities, and coordinates with the designated counterintelligence component to cross-share threat and incident information. Read the sentence backwards and it is an inventory of what disappears when a carve-out is signed: the independent physical inspection, the independent accreditation of the computers, and the independent counterintelligence feed. Its glossary supplies the definition in eleven words of substance: 'carve-out. A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its NISP obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.' Volume 1 also documents two cover mechanisms - HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY (HVSACO), an unclassified handling caveat used among other things 'When using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged SAP', and the rule that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations'.

(2) Authorizes classified contractor SAP information systems (ISs) and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities (SAPFs). (3) Coordinates with the designated counterintelligence (CI) component to provide cross-sharing of threat and incident information affecting the security of the facility or its defense information or cleared personnel.'

DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 10 provides that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations.'

entities.label: The carve-out provision - contractor SAPs exempted from NISP oversight
entities.sub: Mechanism; a SecDef/DepSecDef signature that removes a contractor facility from DCSA industrial security oversight
entities.desc: The carve-out is the most important single mechanism on this board, because it is the point at which a special access program held at a private company stops being visible to any government security official who is not inside the program. It is defined identically in DoD Directive 5205.07 (2010) and DoD Manual 5205.07 Volume 1: 'A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its National Industrial Security Program obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.' It is codified in the National Industrial Security Program rule at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), which provides that 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07'. What is removed is specified in DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1: the SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations, the authorisation of classified contractor SAP information systems and guest systems in contractor SAP facilities, and the coordination with the counterintelligence component for threat and incident cross-sharing. What replaces it is oversight by the cognizant authority's own Program Security Officer - an official appointed by and reporting to the SAP structure itself. The carve-out is requested as line 11.d of the SAP Approval Package Checklist ('Contract strategy (carve-out justification if applicable)'), recommended in the action memo to the Deputy Secretary, and, once approved, must be recorded in the program record file together with 'the identification of SAP facilities ... that have been carved-out based upon this authority'. Neither the number of carve-outs in force, nor the list of carved-out facilities, nor the identity of the approving official for any individual carve-out has ever been published. This is the precise mechanism that would permit a contractor to hold material under a DoD program with no external government inspector ever entering the vault.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3): 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, "DoD SAP Policy".'

The carve-out is approvable only by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense - no delegation to a service secretary, component head or SAPCO director is provided for in DoDD 5205.07 (2010), DoDI 5205.11 or DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1.

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 6 lists 'Proposals to relieve DSS of NISP security oversight responsibilities (carve-out) when required' among the actions that must be coordinated through the DoD SAPCO to the Deputy Secretary of Defense for decision.

DoDI 5205.11 requires DoD SAPCO to provide 'DSS confirmation of SAP facilities where the DSS has been carved out of security oversight functions', which means a list of carved-out facilities exists as an agency record.

After a carve-out, the only recurring security inspection of the contractor facility is conducted by the Program Security Officer, who is 'appointed in writing by the appropriate Director CA SAPCO or designee' and exercises responsibilities 'on behalf of the SAPCO' - that is, by the program inspecting itself. Reasoning: DoDM 5205.07-V1 removes the DSS/DCSA inspection and its glossary defines the PSO's appointment chain as internal to the SAP structure.

entities.label: 32 CFR Part 117 - National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (the NISPOM Rule)
entities.sub: Codified federal regulation, effective 24 February 2021; the baseline security regime a carve-out suspends
entities.desc: The NISPOM ceased to be a DoD manual and became a federal regulation with the codification of 32 CFR Part 117, which now carries the rules binding every cleared contractor in the United States. For this board its value is threefold. First, it supplies the operative regulatory definition of a SAP: 'SAP means any program that is established to control access and distribution and to provide protection for particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required for TOP SECRET, SECRET, or CONFIDENTIAL information. A SAP can be created or continued only as authorized by a senior agency official delegated such authority pursuant to E.O. 13526.' Second, it contains the carve-out at 117.6(b)(3). Third, section 117.23 is the supplement for ACCM, SAPs, SCI, Restricted Data, Formerly Restricted Data, Transclassified Foreign Nuclear Information and Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information, and its paragraph (d)(1) provides that for DoD SAP contracts 'Contractors will implement the security requirements for SAPs codified in SAP-related policy, when established by contract' - a formulation that pushes the actual security rules out of the regulation and into contract documents that are not public. Part 117 also treats SAP information as 'proscribed information' alongside TOP SECRET, COMSEC, Restricted Data and SCI, which triggers the National Interest Determination process for entities under foreign ownership, control or influence. The whole rule is issued under the authority of section 201 of Executive Order 12829.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b): 'SAP means any program that is established to control access and distribution and to provide protection for particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required for TOP SECRET, SECRET, or CONFIDENTIAL information. A SAP can be created or continued only as authorized by a senior agency official delegated such authority pursuant to E.O. 13526.'
32 CFR 117.3(b) lists SAP information as 'proscribed information' together with TOP SECRET information, COMSEC information, Restricted Data and SCI.

32 CFR 117.23(d)(1): 'DoD SAP contracts. Contractors will implement the security requirements for SAPs codified in SAP-related policy, when established by contract. These documents include, but are not limited to, statutes, E.O.s, CSA directives, instructions, manuals, regulations, standards, memorandums, and other SAP security related policy documents.'

32 CFR 117.23(a)(2) provides that where a CSA-created program requires measures exceeding the rule's standards, 'the CSA-imposed higher standards specifically detailed in the contract or conveyed through other applicable directives will be binding on USG and contractor participants.'

32 CFR 117.3(b) defines ACCM as 'security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.'

Because 117.23(d)(1) exports the substantive SAP security requirements into contract documents, the actual rules governing a contractor holding SAP material are not published anywhere in the Code of Federal Regulations and are not obtainable without the contract. Reasoning: the regulation defers to unspecified 'SAP security related policy documents' established by contract.

entities.label: Acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived - the three states of a DoD special access program
entities.sub: Doctrinal taxonomy; each step removes another category of person who is permitted to know
entities.desc: The three-state taxonomy is the vocabulary the whole board depends on, and it is defined word for word in DoD's own issuances. An ACKNOWLEDGED SAP is 'A SAP whose existence is acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to others, but its specific details (technologies, materials, techniques, etc.,) are classified as specified in the applicable SCG'. Its name appears in the budget; you may know that it exists and nothing else. An UNACKNOWLEDGED SAP is 'A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information'. The correct response to an inquiry is neither confirmation nor denial; the program's very existence is classified. A WAIVED SAP is 'A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting in accordance with Reference (c) following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs' - Reference (c) being 10 U.S.C. 119. Cross-cutting the three states are three categories defined by mission: an acquisition SAP protects 'sensitive research, development, testing and evaluation, modification, and procurement activities'; an intelligence SAP protects intelligence activity; and an operations and support SAP is 'established primarily to protect the planning for, execution of, and support to especially sensitive military operations' and 'may protect organizations, property, operational concepts, plans, or activities'. A SAP with subordinate structure is called an 'umbrella', with 'compartments, sub-compartments, or projects' beneath it. The single most important observation for this board is that the alleged legacy recovery effort - if it exists - would sit precisely at the intersection of a waived unacknowledged operations and support SAP with an acquisition SAP for the exploitation work, held under an umbrella whose compartments are known only to the compartment holders. Every element of that description is an ordinary term of art in DoDI 5205.11.

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Glossary: 'acknowledged SAP. A SAP whose existence is acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to others, but its specific details (technologies, materials, techniques, etc.,) are classified as specified in the applicable SCG.'

DoDI 5205.11 Glossary: 'unacknowledged SAP. A SAP having enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.'

DoDI 5205.11 Glossary: 'waived SAP. A SAP for which the SecDef has waived applicable reporting in accordance with Reference (c) following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2010) Glossary: 'operations and support SAP. A SAP established primarily to protect the planning for, execution of, and support to especially sensitive military operations. An operations and support SAP may protect organizations, property, operational concepts, plans, or activities.'
DoDD 5205.07 (2010) Glossary: 'acquisition SAP. A SAP established to protect sensitive research, development, testing and evaluation, modification, and procurement activities.'
DoDI 5205.11 Glossary: 'umbrella. A SAP may also be referred to as an "umbrella" if the SAP has subordinate elements, referred as compartments, sub-compartments, or projects.'

A legacy material-recovery and exploitation effort would map onto the taxonomy as a waived unacknowledged operations and support SAP (recovery and custody of property) with a subordinate acquisition SAP compartment (exploitation and engineering), under a single umbrella. Reasoning: the DoD definitions of operations and support SAP - expressly covering 'property' - and acquisition SAP together describe recovery-plus-reverse-engineering with no strain.

entities.label: The waived unacknowledged SAP - what it actually means in practice
entities.sub: The end state: existence classified, reporting waived, access limited to four to twelve named members
entities.desc: Stack the three documented mechanisms and the result is a program with the following properties, every one of which is sourced to a statute or a DoD issuance rather than to any allegation. Its existence is not acknowledged, affirmed or made known to any person not authorised (DoDI 5205.11 glossary). Its reporting to the defense committees under 10 U.S.C. 119(a), (b) and (c) has been waived by the Secretary of Defense on a case-by-case national-security determination, with the information going instead 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' (10 U.S.C. 119(e)). Within those committees, DoD policy limits access further: members generally 'shall be authorized access to DoD SAPs ... except for waived programs', and for waived programs 'only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors' unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise (DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f). Whatever paper the committee is shown stays in the building: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody' (para 4.h). If the program is executed at a contractor facility, a carve-out approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary removes DCSA inspection, DCSA information-system accreditation and the DCSA counterintelligence feed (32 CFR 117.6(b)(3); DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 2). Fraud, waste, abuse and corruption complaints must be reported 'through SAP channels' and not through collateral channels (DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 4). The Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and recommends to the SAPOC on continued waived status (DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3), so a record of every waived program exists and is reviewed once a year by a body chaired at Principal Deputy Under Secretary level. Nothing in this paragraph is contested. The contested question is only what is inside one of them.

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually. Provides recommendations to the SAPOC concerning continued waived status.'
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the SRG 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report.'
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 2 requires DoD SAPCO to establish 'the criteria for annual reviews of waived DoD SAPs by the SSWG and SRG.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f limits access to waived SAPs, absent SecDef or DepSecDef approval, to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'.

A complete list of waived DoD SAPs demonstrably exists in documentary form, is reviewed at least annually by the Senior Review Group, and is validated by the SAPOC - which means the answer to 'how many waived programs are there' is a retrievable agency record and not an unknowable. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 assigns the annual review of all waived SAPs and the accuracy of the congressional SAP list to a named standing body.

entities.label: Cover mechanisms for unacknowledged SAPs - nicknames, HVSACO, unacknowledged locations
entities.sub: Documented tradecraft by which an unacknowledged program is made invisible in ordinary paperwork and buildings
entities.desc: DoD's own manuals describe, in unclassified text, the tradecraft that keeps an unacknowledged program from surfacing. Every DoD SAP is assigned an unclassified nickname generated through the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff NICKA system under CJCSM 3150.29D, and 'Unclassified nicknames will be used in the annual SAP report to Congress'; whether a classified codeword is also used is decided by the cognizant authority SAPCO. So the artefact Congress receives is a list of two-word nicknames. The marking HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY - HVSACO - is applied, expressly, 'When using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged SAP', and also 'When necessary to protect sensitive relationships' and 'To protect information that does not warrant classification under Executive Order 13526'; the manual states plainly that 'HVSACO is not a classification'. That is a control that restricts distribution of material which is not classified at all, and therefore is not reachable by a mandatory declassification review or by the classification-challenge machinery of E.O. 13526. Physical cover is addressed as well: 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations' - the manual assumes the existence of facilities at which showing a federal badge would itself be a disclosure. Where two programs share a facility, a Co-Utilization Agreement between cognizant security offices governs, and 'For CUAs, the responsible organization will be identified for executing security cognizance with a carved-out SAP', which is how a carved-out program can sit inside a building that other programs also use without the other programs' security officers acquiring cognizance over it.

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 para 5.d: 'All DoD SAPs must be assigned an unclassified nickname generated in accordance with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Manual 3150.29D ... Unclassified nicknames will be used in the annual SAP report to Congress.'
DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 5: HVSACO is applied '(5) When using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged SAP', and 'HVSACO is not a classification.'

DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 5 lists among the purposes of HVSACO 'To preclude the disclosure of general program-related information outside established acknowledged and unacknowledged SAP channels' and 'To minimize OPSEC indicators.'
DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 10 para 5: 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations.'
DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 4 para 4.c: 'For CUAs, the responsible organization will be identified for executing security cognizance with a carved-out SAP.'

Because HVSACO is expressly not a classification, material bearing it is outside the E.O. 13526 declassification system - it cannot be the subject of a mandatory declassification review, an automatic declassification at 25 years, or a classification challenge. Reasoning: those remedies operate only on classified national security information.

entities.label: Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC)
entities.sub: Senior DoD governing body for the SAP enterprise; chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense
entities.desc: The SAPOC was established by DoD Directive 5205.07 on 1 July 2010 to 'advise and assist the Secretary of Defense (SecDef) and the Deputy Secretary of Defense with governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs', and it survives in the 12 September 2024 reissue as 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise'. Under the 2013 instruction its chair is the Deputy Secretary of Defense, its vice-chair the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics, and its executive secretary the Director of DoD SAPCO; its general membership is the Under Secretaries for Policy, Comptroller/CFO, Intelligence, and Personnel and Readiness, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the DoD Chief Information Officer, the General Counsel of the Department, the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Vice Chiefs of Staff of the Army and Air Force, the Vice Chief of Naval Operations and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps. Its three primary functions are to review issues on which the Senior Review Group could not reach unanimity, to ensure combatant command warfighting needs are reflected in SAP programmatics and budgets, and - the function that matters here - to 'Conduct an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees'. In other words, the document Congress receives about special access programs is written and validated by a committee of roughly eighteen senior officials of the Department the report is about, chaired by the same official who signs the carve-outs. This is the body whose membership a witness alleging concealment would have to say was either complicit or itself deceived; DoD's own directive makes that a binary with no third option.

claims.text: DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.b: 'The Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC), hereby established, shall advise and assist the Secretary of Defense (SecDef) and the Deputy Secretary of Defense with governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs.'

DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3: SAPOC membership is Chair - the Deputy Secretary of Defense; Vice-Chair - USD(AT&L); Executive Secretary - Director, DoD SAPCO; with general membership USD(P), USD(C)/CFO, USD(I), USD(P&R), the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, DoD CIO, GC DoD, DCAPE, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Vice Chiefs of Staff of the Army and Air Force, the Vice Chief of Naval Operations and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps.

DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 para 2.b(3): the SAPOC convenes at the direction of the Deputy Secretary of Defense to 'Conduct an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees.'

DoDD 5205.07 (12 September 2024) retains the SAPOC as 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise for governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs', chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

Because the SAPOC both validates the congressional SAP report and sits under the official who approves carve-outs and waivers, the Department's account of its own special access programs is produced entirely inside the compartment it describes, with no external validator at any point. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 gives the annual validation to the SAPOC and no issuance assigns any external body a concurrent validation role.

entities.label: Senior Review Group (DoD SAP governance)
entities.sub: Working-level body that reviews every SAP establishment, every carve-out proposal and every waived program annually
entities.desc: The Senior Review Group is described in DoDI 5205.11 as 'the principal working-level body executing the governance process and performing oversight and management of DoD SAPs', and its unanimous recommendations 'may be forwarded directly to the DepSecDef for decision' - bypassing the SAPOC entirely. It is chaired by the Principal Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics, vice-chaired by the Director of DoD SAPCO and with the Deputy Director of DoD SAPCO as executive secretary; its members are the primary or alternate representatives designated in writing by each SAPOC member, with the Army, Navy and Air Force each casting a single vote. It convenes at the direction of the Deputy Secretary to review proposals to establish or disestablish SAPs, designate cognizant and oversight authorities, remove DoD programs from special access controls, apportion SAPs into and out of integrated joint special technical operations, alter the scope, category or type of a SAP, approve the use of DoD resources to support DoD and non-DoD SAPs, and review foreign access and participation. Two of its enumerated functions are decisive for this board: it 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and provides recommendations on continued waived status, and it 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report'. If a waived program existed that was not on the list submitted to Congress, the SRG is the body that would have had to certify a list it knew to be incomplete - or the body from which the program was itself concealed.

entities.label: SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG)
entities.sub: Deconfliction forum chaired by the Director of DoD SAPCO; the first body a new program meets
entities.desc: The SSWG is the lowest of the three governance tiers and the one that sees a prospective program first: under the PSAP timeline, the SSWG reviews a prospective SAP no later than fourteen days after its establishment, performing programmatic deconfliction and validation and producing a written recommendation. It 'serves as the senior program protection forum to coordinate, deconflict, and integrate special programs; address SAP policy, oversight, and management; and provide recommendations to the SRG'. It is chaired by the Director of DoD SAPCO, with members the SAPCO Directors of USD(I), USD(P), USD(AT&L), the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps, the Joint Staff, DARPA and the Missile Defense Agency, plus representatives of DCAPE, the DoD CIO, the Comptroller and the General Counsel. The presence of DARPA and MDA SAPCO directors on the deconfliction forum is worth noting for the board: those are two of the organisations most frequently named in retrieval and exploitation allegations, and their SAP control offices sit at the table where every new program is deconflicted against every existing one.

entities.desc: DoD SAPCO is established by directive 'under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense' and is 'the primary DoD liaison with agencies of the Executive Branch and the Congress on all issues relating to DoD SAPs'; its Director 'shall be a flag officer or Senior Executive Service equivalent appointed by the Deputy Secretary of Defense'. The 2013 instruction adds that the Director 'Functions as the DoD single point of Congressional liaison concerning SAPs', chairs the SSWG, vice-chairs the SRG, serves as Executive Secretary of the SAPOC, establishes the criteria for the annual review of waived SAPs, establishes 'policies and applicable procedures to satisfy reporting requirements for DSS carve-outs', and provides 'DSS confirmation of SAP facilities where the DSS has been carved out of security oversight functions'. The structural consequence is that a single office, whose director is appointed by and reports to the official who signs waivers and carve-outs, sits between every DoD special access program and every member of Congress, and is the office that must be notified whenever anyone accessed to a DoD SAP briefs a member. No DoD SAPCO director has ever testified in open session, and the identity of the incumbent director is not published.

entities.desc: DCSA, the successor to the Defense Security Service, is designated by 32 CFR 117.6(b)(1) as the DoD Cognizant Security Office. It administers the National Industrial Security Program 'as a separate program element on behalf of DoD GCAs and those agencies with agreements with DoD for security services' and 'Provides security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO on behalf of DoD components and those non-DoD executive branch agencies who enter into agreements with DoD'. It issues facility clearances for defense contractors 'to include contractors performing on DoD SAPs'. It is the only recurring, external, adversarial security inspection that a cleared contractor facility receives - and it is the entity that the carve-out provision at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) switches off by a signature of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense. entities.label: Intelligence Community Directive 906, Controlled Access Programs
entities.sub: ODNI directive; the intelligence community's counterpart to the DoD SAP regime, with no statutory reporting clock at all
entities.desc: ICD 906 is the directive that governs what the intelligence community calls its special access programs. Its authority is 'The National Security Act of 1947, as amended; Executive Order (EO) 12333, as amended; and other applicable provisions of law', and it 'establishes the oversight and management of Intelligence Community (IC) special access programs pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document, referred to within the IC as Controlled Access Programs (CAPs)'. The reissued version obtained for this board supersedes the ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015; the released PDF was generated on 19 December 2024 and its signature block is an image that does not resolve to text, so the exact reissue date is not machine-readable in the public copy. The substance is unambiguous and, for this board, extraordinary. Only the DNI or the Principal Deputy DNI may establish, validate, modify or terminate a CAP. CAPs are defined as 'a top-level control system (such as Special Intelligence, Talent Keyhole, Human Intelligence Control System), and any compartment or sub-compartment under a control system'. Unacknowledged CAPs exist and 'may be established only where knowledge of the existence of a program would reveal aspects of its protected information ... Unacknowledged CAPs may be established only with the approval of the DNI or PDDNI'. Governance mirrors DoD: a CAP Oversight Committee chaired by the PDDNI or designee, and a Senior Review Group. All CAPs are to be recorded in Scattered Castles, the IC personnel security database - 'Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI'. Access may be limited by billet or 'by name or position (BYNOP)'. Critically, ICD 906 assigns the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office responsibility for 'the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council' - and nowhere in the directive is there any counterpart to 10 U.S.C. 119: no annual report deadline, no 30-day pre-initiation notice, no statutory list. The IC side of the architecture has less congressional reporting machinery than the DoD side, not more. ICD 906 also expressly does not apply to SAPs established by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, 'Nor does this Directive apply to special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action' - identifying, in one sentence, a third category of program governed by neither regime.

ICD 906 section C.3: the directive does not apply to SAPs established by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, and 'Nor does this Directive apply to special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.'

ICD 906 section D.3: 'unacknowledged CAPs may be established only where knowledge of the existence of a program would reveal aspects of its protected information ... Unacknowledged CAPs may be established only with the approval of the DNI or PDDNI.'

ICD 906 section D.2 defines CAPs as 'a top-level control system (such as Special Intelligence, Talent Keyhole, Human Intelligence Control System), and any compartment or sub-compartment under a control system within the IC.'

ICD 906 section D.6 requires all CAPs and individual accesses to be recorded in Scattered Castles or its successor, and provides that 'Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.'

ICD 906 section D.7 establishes a CAP Oversight Committee (CAPOC) chaired by the PDDNI or designee, responsible for oversight of CAPs 'to include all unacknowledged CAPs'; section D.8 establishes a Senior Review Group.

ICD 906 section D.5 requires CAP information to be discoverable or exempted from discovery under ICD 501, and provides that 'Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.'
ICD 906 contains no annual congressional reporting deadline, no pre-initiation notification period and no statutory reporting clock equivalent to 10 U.S.C. 119.

entities.desc: CAPCO is the intelligence community's counterpart to DoD SAPCO and does two distinct jobs. Under ICD 906 the Director of the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office is 'the accountable official responsible for the implementation of this policy', serves as central point of contact for all CAP requirements, and must 'Manage a CAP Registry that maintains a list of all control systems, including all compartments and sub-compartments', deconflict all IC CAPs against all other programs, and 'manage all compartment and sub compartment names, codenames, and any other pertinent information'. It is also 'responsible for the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council' - the same choke-point design as DoD SAPCO, with ISOO's access routed through the office whose programs ISOO would be examining. Separately, CAPCO publishes the Intelligence Community Authorized Classification and Control Markings Register and Manual, the document that defines the entire marking syntax used across the U.S. classification system, including the Special Access Program marking category. For this board the CAP Registry is the single most valuable unreleased document in the intelligence community: a complete list of every control system, compartment and sub-compartment, maintained by name, in one office, by directive.

entities.label: IC Authorized Classification and Control Markings Register and Manual (the CAPCO Register)
entities.sub: CAPCO-published marking standard; defines the SAR- Special Access Required marking and hides part of itself
entities.desc: The CAPCO Register is the rulebook for how classified material is marked across the United States government, and reading it tells you how a special access program looks on paper. The publicly released Volume 5, Edition 1 (Version 5.1), effective 30 December 2011 with an administrative update of 30 March 2012, establishes a distinct Special Access Program Markings category - moved in that edition out of the Non-Intelligence Community Dissemination Control Markings category - which follows the SCI control markings in the banner line. 'The first value in the SAP category is the SAP category indicator either "SPECIAL ACCESS REQUIRED-" or "SAR-" (the authorized abbreviation) ... Following the SAP category indicator shall be the SAP program indicator which is the program's nickname or authorized digraph or trigraph.' Compartments follow the program identifier separated by hyphens; sub-compartments follow the compartment. That syntax is why the sample DoD action memo in DoDI 5205.11 is marked '(S//SAR-GTE)'. The Register was produced by CAPCO with the IC Classification Markings Implementation Working Group, whose members include the Air Force, Army, CIA, Coast Guard, DEA, DHS, DIA, DOE, State, FBI, Marine Corps, Navy, NGA, NRO, NSA, ODNI, OUSD(I) and Treasury, advised by NARA's Information Security Oversight Office. And the title page of the public version carries the note that settles a recurring argument: 'Certain security markings were removed due to classified content. These markings have been compiled in separate classified addenda.' The public register is therefore known, on its own face, to be incomplete - there exist compartment markings whose very existence is classified, listed in addenda that have never been released.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. Sec. 3348 - SAP reporting for every agency that is not DoD, NNSA or IC
entities.sub: FY1994 NDAA sec. 1152; supplies the only statutory definition of 'special access program' and names House Oversight
entities.desc: Section 1152 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1994, Public Law 103-160 of 30 November 1993, now codified at 50 U.S.C. 3348, is the sleeper statute of this whole architecture and it is almost never cited in UAP reporting. It imposes on the head of every 'covered department or agency' the same February 1 annual report, new-program notice, 14-day declassification notice and 30-day report-and-wait that 10 U.S.C. 119 imposes on the Secretary of Defense - and it defines 'covered department or agency' as 'any department or agency of the Federal Government that carries out a special access program', excluding only DoD (covered by 10 U.S.C. 119), the National Nuclear Security Administration (covered by 50 U.S.C. 2426) and 'an agency in the Intelligence Community'. Two provisions make it invaluable. First, it supplies the statutory definition of a special access program: 'any program that, under the authority of Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order), is established by the head of a department or agency whom the President has designated in the Federal Register as an original "secret" or "top secret" classification authority that imposes "need-to-know" controls or access controls beyond those controls normally required ... for access to information classified as "confidential", "secret", or "top secret".' Second, as amended by section 103 of Public Law 115-390 on 21 December 2018, 'congressional oversight committees' means 'congressional leadership and authorizing and appropriations congressional committees with jurisdiction or shared jurisdiction over a department or agency', the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, AND the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives. The House Oversight Committee - the committee that has run the public UAP hearings since July 2023 - is a named statutory recipient of special access program reports from every covered agency. And its waiver provision, subsection (e)(2), does not narrow the audience: the waived information still goes 'to the congressional oversight committees', not to a chair and ranking member. The non-defense SAP reporting regime is materially stronger than DoD's.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3) defines 'special access program' as 'any program that, under the authority of Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order), is established by the head of a department or agency whom the President has designated in the Federal Register as an original "secret" or "top secret" classification authority that imposes "need-to-know" controls or access controls beyond those controls normally required ... for access to information classified as "confidential", "secret", or "top secret".'

50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(1) defines 'congressional oversight committees' to include 'the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives' and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, as well as congressional leadership and the authorizing and appropriations committees with jurisdiction.

50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2): where the waiver is exercised, the agency head 'shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, to the congressional oversight committees' - the full committees, not a chair and ranking member.
50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) excludes from 'covered department or agency' only the Department of Defense, the National Nuclear Security Administration and agencies in the Intelligence Community.

Section 3348 was enacted as Pub. L. 103-160, div. A, title XI, sec. 1152, 30 November 1993, 107 Stat. 1758, and amended by Pub. L. 115-390, sec. 103, 21 December 2018, which substituted 'the congressional oversight committees' for 'Congress' throughout and added the definition of that term.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. Sec. 2426 - NNSA special access programs, and the only waiver that reaches the 30-day clock
entities.sub: FY2000 NDAA sec. 3236; the nuclear-weapons complex SAP reporting regime, with a stronger waiver than DoD's
entities.desc: Section 3236 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2000, Public Law 106-65, created a separate SAP reporting regime for the National Nuclear Security Administration, now at 50 U.S.C. 2426. Structurally it is a copy of 10 U.S.C. 119: a February 1 annual report to the congressional defense committees, a February 1 new-program notice with justification, a 14-day notice before a classification change or public declassification, prompt notice of changes to designation criteria, and a 30-day report-and-wait before initiation. But subsection (e)(1) is materially broader than the DoD waiver. It gives the Administrator the same power to waive the reporting requirements of subsections (a), (b) and (c), and then adds a sentence that has no counterpart in title 10: 'The Administrator may waive the report-and-wait requirement in subsection (f) if the Administrator determines that compliance with such requirement would adversely affect the national security.' Under 10 U.S.C. 119 the Secretary of Defense may waive what he tells the committees but not the requirement to notify them thirty days before starting a program. Under 50 U.S.C. 2426 the Administrator of the NNSA may waive both. That is the single most permissive SAP provision in the United States Code, and it sits in the statute governing the agency that runs the weapons laboratories - Los Alamos, Sandia, Lawrence Livermore - and holds Restricted Data under the Atomic Energy Act. The waived information goes 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees'.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(1): 'The Administrator may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) ... The Administrator may waive the report-and-wait requirement in subsection (f) if the Administrator determines that compliance with such requirement would adversely affect the national security. Any waiver under this paragraph shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'
50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(2) directs the waived information and justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.'

50 U.S.C. 2426(f) otherwise imposes the same 30-day report-and-wait as 10 U.S.C. 119(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated until - (1) the congressional defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.'
Section 2426 was enacted by Pub. L. 106-65, div. C, title XXXII, sec. 3236, 5 October 1999, 113 Stat. 962, and amended by Pub. L. 113-291, sec. 3143(b), 19 December 2014.

The NNSA Administrator can lawfully initiate a special access program with no advance notice to any congressional committee, because the waiver in 2426(e)(1) expressly reaches the report-and-wait requirement of 2426(f); the Secretary of Defense cannot, because 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) reaches only subsections (a), (b) and (c). Reasoning: direct textual comparison of the two waiver provisions.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. Sec. 3091a - congressional oversight of Controlled Access Programs
entities.sub: National Security Act sec. 501A, added 2022 and hardened in 2024; the only SAP-type regime with no waiver and a funding cutoff
entities.desc: Section 501A of the National Security Act of 1947 was added by section 504 of the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-103 of 15 March 2022, and is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3091a. It is the statutory counterpart to ICD 906, and it defines 'controlled access program' by direct reference: 'a program created or managed pursuant to Intelligence Community Directive 906, or successor directive' - the United States Code citing an ODNI directive by URL. As enacted it required the DNI to brief the intelligence committees and congressional leadership on every controlled access program in effect not less than semiannually or on request, prohibited the head of an IC element from establishing a CAP or any compartment or subcompartment within one until the appropriate committees and leadership are notified, and required annual reports listing all active and all terminated compartments and subcompartments, with a DNI certification for each that its creation, validation or substantial modification is 'substantiated and justified', the identification of a control officer for each program, and a statement of protection requirements. Then, on 23 December 2024, sections 6602 and 6603 of the FY2025 NDAA, Public Law 118-159, added two teeth. Section 6602 inserted a new subsection (c): National Intelligence Program funds 'may not be obligated or expended for any controlled access program, or a compartment or subcompartment therein' until the required notification is submitted. Section 6603 added subsection (b)(2), prohibiting the head of an IC element from transferring 'a capability from a controlled access program, including from a compartment or subcompartment therein to a compartment or subcompartment of another controlled access program, to a special access program (as defined in section 3348(g) of this title), or to anything else outside the controlled access program' without prior notice - subject to exceptions for 'an urgent counterintelligence issue' or 'an organizational restructuring'. That second provision is Congress legislating directly against the mechanism at the centre of this board: moving a capability out of one compartment regime and into another to break the audit trail. Congress does not write a statute against a manoeuvre nobody has performed.

50 U.S.C. 3091a(b)(2)(A), added by Pub. L. 118-159 sec. 6603 (23 December 2024): a head of an IC element 'may not transfer a capability from a controlled access program, including from a compartment or subcompartment therein to a compartment or subcompartment of another controlled access program, to a special access program (as defined in section 3348(g) of this title), or to anything else outside the controlled access program, until the head submits to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership notice of the intent of the head to make such transfer.'

50 U.S.C. 3091a(b)(2)(B) permits transfer without prior notification where the head determines it 'is required to mitigate an urgent counterintelligence issue' or 'is necessary to maintain access in the event of an organizational restructuring.'

50 U.S.C. 3091a(c), added by Pub. L. 118-159 sec. 6602: NIP funds 'may not be obligated or expended for any controlled access program, or a compartment or subcompartment therein, until the head of the element ... submits the notification required by subsection (b).'

50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(2) requires each annual report to list all active compartments and subcompartments, all terminated during the period, and for the DNI a certification that creation, validation or substantial modification of every program is 'substantiated and justified', with 'the identification of a control officer for each controlled access program' and 'a statement of protection requirements'.
Section 3091a contains no waiver authority of any kind.

entities.label: The four SAP reporting regimes and the seam between them
entities.sub: Comparative analysis; DoD's waiver is the weakest link in a system of four parallel statutes
entities.desc: There is no single United States statute on special access programs. There are four parallel regimes plus covert action, and the differences between them are where a program can live. (1) DoD - 10 U.S.C. 119: annual report by 1 March, new-program notice by 1 February, 14-day declassification notice, 30-day report-and-wait, all to six defense committees; the Secretary may waive the reports on a national-security determination, in which case the information goes only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each. (2) NNSA - 50 U.S.C. 2426: identical structure to the defense committees, but the Administrator may additionally waive the 30-day report-and-wait itself. (3) Every other agency - 50 U.S.C. 3348: identical structure, but reporting runs to 'congressional oversight committees' expressly including House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security, and the waiver does not narrow the audience. (4) The Intelligence Community - 50 U.S.C. 3091a and ICD 906: no annual statutory deadline and no waiver at all, but semiannual briefings on every program, a prohibition on establishment before notification, a funding cutoff since December 2024, and a prohibition on transferring capabilities out of a CAP into a SAP without notice since December 2024. Set beside each other, the ranking is unambiguous: the weakest reporting regime in the United States government belongs to the Department of Defense, and it is weakest precisely at the point where the Secretary decides how much to tell the committees. Two structural seams follow. The first is between regimes: a capability transferred from an IC controlled access program to a DoD special access program changes which statute governs it and which committees see it - the manoeuvre Congress prohibited prospectively in December 2024, three decades after the alleged conduct. The second is around all four: ICD 906 section C.3 records that none of them applies to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action', which are governed only by 50 U.S.C. 3093 and its Gang of Eight.

claims.text: Four separate statutes govern SAP-type reporting: 10 U.S.C. 119 (DoD), 50 U.S.C. 2426 (NNSA), 50 U.S.C. 3348 (all other non-IC agencies) and 50 U.S.C. 3091a (IC controlled access programs).

Of the four regimes, only 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and 50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(2) narrow the recipient of waived information to the chairman and ranking minority member; 50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2) keeps the full oversight committees, and 50 U.S.C. 3091a has no waiver provision at all.

A program moved between the DoD and IC regimes changes both its governing statute and its reporting audience, and before 23 December 2024 no statute required notice of the move. That is a documented, lawful, unnotified route by which a program's oversight history can be broken. Reasoning: the prohibition added by Pub.
