entities.label: The Gang of Eight and the limited-notification convention
entities.sub: Statutory notification group for covert action under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2); the model for every 'four members were told' claim
entities.desc: The phrase 'Gang of Eight' has a precise statutory origin that is routinely misapplied to special access programs, and getting it right matters. Under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(1) a presidential finding authorising covert action must be reported in writing to the congressional intelligence committees as soon as possible after approval and before initiation. Paragraph (2) is the exception: 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.' Four committee leaders plus four chamber leaders: eight. Since the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2010, paragraph (5)(A) requires a written statement of the reasons for limiting access, and (5)(B) requires that within 180 days either all members of the intelligence committees get access or a further written statement of reasons is submitted. Paragraph (3) preserves the option of no prior notice at all, requiring only that the President 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' afterwards with a statement of reasons. The DoD waived-SAP convention is a different animal that behaves the same way: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees', and DoD Directive 5205.07 (2010) restricted access for waived programs to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'. The DoD version has no 180-day sunset, no requirement to widen access ever, and no statutory statement-of-reasons requirement beyond the waiver justification itself. On paper, covert action is better supervised than a waived special access program.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2): 'If the President determines that it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.'

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a statement of reasons for limited access, the President ensure either that all members of the intelligence committees are provided access to the finding or notification, or that a further statement of reasons is submitted to the Gang of Eight.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported under paragraph (1) or (2) at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice.'

50 U.S.C. 3091(e): 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.'

The covert action regime contains a mandatory 180-day review of continued limited access; the DoD waived-SAP regime contains no equivalent, so a waived DoD program can remain restricted to a handful of members indefinitely with no statutory event ever forcing reconsideration. Reasoning: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

entities.label: FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687 - Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs
entities.sub: Public Law 118-31, 22 December 2023; Congress cuts off money for unreported UAP special access activity
entities.desc: Section 1687 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 is the moment the SAP architecture and the UAP question meet in enacted law. Subsection (a): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Subsection (b) closes the industry-funded route: consistent with DoD Instruction 3204.01, 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership'. The definitions widen the audience well past 10 U.S.C. 119(g): 'appropriate congressional committees' means the congressional defense committees plus both intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' means the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. Three things follow. First, Congress enacted, on 22 December 2023, a funding prohibition premised on the possibility that UAP activity was being run under special access or restricted access limitations without being reported - a premise it would not have legislated against had it been satisfied no such activity existed. Second, subsection (b) targets precisely the mechanism by which a contractor can fund work internally and recover it as overhead, which is the route that does not appear in any appropriation line. Third, by naming the AARO fiscal year 2024 report, Congress tied the prohibition to a specific document rather than leaving it abstract.

claims.text: FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687(a): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.'

FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687(b): 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 ... independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' The subsection is noted as 50 U.S.C. 3373 note.

FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687(c) defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and 'congressional leadership' as the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House.

Section 1687 is a legislative admission that Congress could not rule out the existence of UAP activity protected by special access or restricted access limitations and unreported to it as of December 2023. Reasoning: a funding prohibition conditioned on disclosure has no operative effect unless the conditioned conduct is considered possible.

entities.desc: Division G of Public Law 118-31 is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, and its section 7343 mirrors section 1687 on the intelligence side with a different addressee and a wider committee list. Subsection (b): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this division may be obligated or expended in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Its 'appropriate committees of Congress' are the Select Committee on Intelligence, the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate, and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations of the House - six committees, plus the four congressional leaders. Subsection (c) carries the same independent research and development prohibition. Read together, sections 1687 and 7343 mean that as of 22 December 2023 both the Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence are under a statutory funding prohibition for unreported UAP special access activity, and both prohibitions run to a combined audience far wider than the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver group. Congress did not repeal the waiver; it built a subject-matter carve-out around it.

entities.label: The annual DoD special access program report to Congress
entities.sub: The recurring artefact required by 10 U.S.C. 119(a); a list of nicknames, validated inside the Department
entities.desc: The annual SAP report is the single document that would settle the central question of this board, and everything about how it is produced is documented. It is required by 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) by 1 March each year to the six defense committees, and must set out the total requested for DoD SAPs and, for each program in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual prior cost, and estimated cost across six fiscal years. DoDI 5205.11 assigns its production: the cognizant authorities 'shall prepare and submit annual reports and other required SAP information through the Director, DoD SAPCO, and the governance structure in order to report the state of DoD SAPs to congressional committees'; the Senior Review Group 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report'; and the SAPOC conducts 'an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees'. The report is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs under DoDI 5545.02. Programs identified in it are identified by unclassified nickname. Waived programs are, by definition, the ones removed from it under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), with their information going instead to eight to twelve named members; and under DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.h the waived material 'shall remain in DoD custody' with no copies stored outside DoD repositories. The report has never been released, in whole or in redacted part, under FOIA. It is the highest value single target on the board: one document, produced annually since 1988, whose table of contents is the answer.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1)-(2) require the annual SAP report by 1 March with the total amount requested and, for each SAP in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual prior-year costs and six years of cost estimates.

DoDI 5205.11 para 5.d: 'Unclassified nicknames will be used in the annual SAP report to Congress.'

The annual SAP report has existed as a recurring agency record since the first one was due on 1 February 1988 under the original text of 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1), and its accuracy is certified annually by two named standing bodies - which makes 'nobody knows how many SAPs there are' a false statement about a document that exists in roughly forty annual editions. Reasoning: the statutory deadline plus the SRG and SAPOC validation functions.

entities.label: Alternative Compensatory Control Measures (ACCM)
entities.sub: Sub-SAP compartmentation with no statutory reporting requirement whatsoever
entities.desc: ACCM is the layer below a special access program, and it is the layer with no statute attached to it at all. The NISPOM rule defines it: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.' The rule then requires contractors to implement ACCM protection requirements 'when established by contract, in accordance with applicable statutes, E.O.s, CSA directives, instructions, manuals, regulations, standards, and memorandums', and covers ACCM in the same supplement, section 117.23, as SAPs, SCI and Restricted Data. The importance for this board is precise and narrow: ACCM produces access lists, nicknames and compartmented handling that look and function like a special access program, but because it is by definition the case 'where SAP controls are not required', an ACCM is not a SAP, and therefore nothing in 10 U.S.C. 119 applies to it. There is no annual ACCM report to the defense committees, no new-ACCM notice, no 30-day report-and-wait and no waiver to exercise, because there is nothing to waive. An activity that needs compartmentation but does not want a line in the annual SAP report has a documented, lawful place to sit.

claims.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b): 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.'
32 CFR 117.23 addresses ACCM in the same supplement as SAPs, SCI, RD, FRD, TFNI and NNPI, requiring contractors to implement ACCM protection requirements 'when established by contract'.

Because ACCM is defined as the case where SAP controls are not required, an ACCM is outside the definition of 'special access program' in 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3), and therefore outside every SAP congressional reporting statute. Reasoning: all four reporting statutes are triggered by the term 'special access program', which ACCM expressly is not.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. Sec. 3093 - Presidential approval and reporting of covert actions
entities.sub: National Security Act sec. 503; the covert action finding regime and the statutory home of the Gang of Eight
entities.desc: Section 503 of the National Security Act of 1947, added by the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1991, Public Law 102-88 of 14 August 1991, governs the one category of activity that sits outside every special access program reporting regime. ICD 906 section C.3 states in terms that neither it nor the DoD SAP regime applies to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action'. Section 3093 requires a written presidential finding before any covert action, reported in writing to the intelligence committees 'as soon as possible after such approval and before the initiation of the covert action'. Subsection (c)(2) is the exception the press calls the Gang of Eight: where the President determines it essential to limit access 'to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States', the finding may go to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and any other leadership members the President chooses to include. Subsection (c)(3) permits no prior notice at all, requiring only that the President afterwards 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with a statement of reasons. Subsection (c)(5), added in 2010, requires a written statement of reasons for limiting access and forces a reconsideration within 180 days - a protection with no counterpart in the SAP statutes. Subsection (d) extends the same notification rules to 'any significant change in a previously approved covert action' and lists the factors that make an undertaking significant, including whether it 'requires an expansion of existing authorities, including authorities relating to research, development, or operations' and whether it 'results in the expenditure of significant funds or other resources'. For this board the importance is structural: an activity characterised as covert action under NSC purview is reportable only under section 3093, is invisible to the defense committees entirely, and can lawfully be known to as few as eight members of Congress - or, under (c)(3), to none in advance.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) permits a covert action finding to be reported to 'the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.'

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported in advance at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice'.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limited access the President ensure that all members of the intelligence committees get access, or submit a further statement of reasons.

50 U.S.C. 3093(d)(2) lists among the factors making an undertaking significant whether it 'requires an expansion of existing authorities, including authorities relating to research, development, or operations' and whether it 'results in the expenditure of significant funds or other resources'.
ICD 906 section C.3 records that the IC controlled access program regime does not apply to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action'.

An activity characterised as covert action is reportable to no defense committee at all, and under 3093(c)(3) need not be reported to anyone in advance - making it the only regime weaker on prior notice than a waived DoD special access program. Reasoning: 3093 runs solely to the intelligence committees or the Gang of Eight, and (c)(3) removes even that.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. Sec. 3091 - General congressional oversight of intelligence activities
entities.sub: National Security Act sec. 501; the 'fully and currently informed' duty and the anti-withholding rule
entities.desc: Section 501 of the National Security Act, at 50 U.S.C. 3091, is the general obligation against which every claim of concealment from Congress in the intelligence sphere must be measured. Subsection (a)(1) requires the President to 'ensure that the congressional intelligence committees are kept fully and currently informed of the intelligence activities of the United States, including any significant anticipated intelligence activity'. Subsection (b) requires that 'any illegal intelligence activity is reported promptly to the congressional intelligence committees, as well as any corrective action that has been taken or is planned'. And subsection (e) closes the classification defence completely: 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.' That sentence is the most useful single line of statute for anyone arguing that a compartment cannot lawfully be used to keep the intelligence committees out of an intelligence activity. Its limits are equally important: it binds only as to intelligence activities and only as to the intelligence committees, so it does not reach a DoD acquisition or operations and support special access program, and it does not reach the defense committees at all.

claims.text: 50 U.S.C. 3091(a)(1): 'The President shall ensure that the congressional intelligence committees are kept fully and currently informed of the intelligence activities of the United States, including any significant anticipated intelligence activity as required by this subchapter.'

50 U.S.C. 3091(e): 'Nothing in this chapter shall be construed as authority to withhold information from the congressional intelligence committees on the grounds that providing the information to the congressional intelligence committees would constitute the unauthorized disclosure of classified information or information relating to intelligence sources and methods.'
50 U.S.C. 3091(b) requires that any illegal intelligence activity be reported promptly to the congressional intelligence committees together with corrective action taken or planned.
50 U.S.C. 3091(f) provides that 'intelligence activities' includes covert actions as defined in section 3093(e) and financial intelligence activities.

Section 3091(e) forbids using classification as a reason to withhold from the intelligence committees, but it operates only on 'intelligence activities' and only for those committees, so a DoD operations and support or acquisition special access program is outside its reach entirely. Reasoning: the duty is defined by the subject matter 'intelligence activities' and the audience 'congressional intelligence committees'.

timeline.label: Congress first requires DoD to report special access programs
timeline.text: President Reagan signs Public Law 100-180. Section 1132(a)(1) adds section 119 to title 10, creating for the first time a statutory duty to tell the defense committees that a special access program exists. Every alleged legacy activity from the 1940s to this date ran under no SAP reporting obligation at all. The same section creates the subsection (e) waiver in the same breath.

timeline.label: The government-wide SAP statute and the only statutory definition
timeline.text: Section 1152 of the FY1994 NDAA, Public Law 103-160, imposes the same reporting regime on every federal agency that runs a SAP other than DoD, the nuclear weapons complex and the intelligence community, and supplies the only statutory definition of 'special access program' in the United States Code, now at 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3).

timeline.label: Executive Order 12829 creates the National Industrial Security Program
timeline.text: The order directs the Secretary of Defense to issue and maintain the NISP Operating Manual and designates the Defense Security Service as the DoD Cognizant Security Office - creating the inspection function that a carve-out would later switch off.

timeline.label: NNSA gets a SAP statute with a broader waiver than DoD's
timeline.text: Section 3236 of the FY2000 NDAA, Public Law 106-65, creates 50 U.S.C. 2426. Its subsection (e)(1) lets the NNSA Administrator waive not only the reports but the 30-day report-and-wait itself - the most permissive SAP provision in the Code, governing the agency that holds Restricted Data and runs Los Alamos, Sandia and Livermore.

timeline.label: GAO audits contractor security and is steered around special access programs
timeline.text: GAO-04-332 finds that DoD 'cannot provide adequate assurances that its oversight ensures the protection of classified information' at more than 11,000 cleared contractor facilities. Footnote 2 records that, by agreement with committee staff, the review 'did not include DSS's oversight of special access programs at contractor facilities.'

timeline.label: Executive Order 13526 fixes the six officials who may create a SAP
timeline.text: Section 4.3 limits SAP creation to the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General and the DNI, or their principal deputies, requires the number to be kept at an absolute minimum, and affords the ISOO Director access 'consistent with the policies and procedures directed by the President'.

timeline.label: DoD Directive 5205.07 defines acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived
timeline.text: The directive establishes the SAPOC and DoD SAPCO and puts the three-state taxonomy into DoD policy in terms, together with the rule that committee members get access to DoD SAPs 'except for waived programs' and that waived material submitted to Congress 'shall remain in DoD custody'.

timeline.label: CAPCO Register v5.1 gives SAPs their own marking category
timeline.text: Volume 5 Edition 1 of the IC Authorized Classification and Control Markings Register moves the Special Access Required marking into a dedicated Special Access Program Markings category with the indicator 'SAR-'. Its title page records that certain markings were removed for classification and 'compiled in separate classified addenda'.

timeline.label: DoDI 5205.11 publishes the carve-out request procedure and a worked example
timeline.text: The instruction sets the prospective SAP timeline ending 'NLT P+210 - End of 30-day period without Congressional decision', requires a carve-out justification in the approval package, and reproduces a sample action memo to the Deputy Secretary recommending that a fictional unacknowledged SAP be approved and that 'The Defense Security Service will be carved out from its normal industrial security oversight responsibilities.'

timeline.label: ICD 906 signed, governing Controlled Access Programs
timeline.text: The DNI's directive establishes the IC's counterpart to the DoD SAP regime, defines CAPs as control systems with compartments and sub-compartments, permits unacknowledged CAPs on DNI or PDDNI approval, and creates the CAP Oversight Committee and Senior Review Group. This version was later superseded by a reissue released in December 2024.

timeline.label: DoD SAP Security Manual Volume 1 issued
timeline.text: DoDM 5205.07-V1 states what a carve-out removes - contractor SAP security inspections, information system authorisation and counterintelligence cross-sharing - and defines carve-out in its glossary as a provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary that relieves DSS of its NISP obligation.

timeline.label: House Oversight named a statutory recipient of SAP reports
timeline.text: Section 103 of Public Law 115-390 amends 50 U.S.C. 3348 to substitute 'the congressional oversight committees' for 'Congress' throughout and defines that term to include the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

timeline.label: The NISPOM becomes federal regulation at 32 CFR Part 117
timeline.text: The carve-out provision moves from a DoD manual into the Code of Federal Regulations at 117.6(b)(3): the Director, DCSA 'will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision'.

timeline.label: Congress creates a statutory oversight regime for IC Controlled Access Programs
timeline.text: Section 504 of the FY2022 Intelligence Authorization Act, Public Law 117-103, adds section 501A to the National Security Act: semiannual briefings on every CAP, a prohibition on establishing a CAP or compartment before notification, and annual reports listing every active and terminated compartment with a DNI certification for each.

timeline.label: Congress cuts off money for unreported UAP special access activity
timeline.text: Sections 1687 and 7343 of Public Law 118-31 bar the obligation of funds for any UAP activity 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' unless the Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence respectively provide details to the defense and intelligence committees and congressional leadership, and make UAP-related independent research and development unallowable as an indirect expense.

timeline.label: DoD deletes acknowledged, unacknowledged, waived and carve-out from its SAP directive
timeline.text: The reissued DoD Directive 5205.07 cancels the 2010 version, incorporates the 11 July 2023 SAP Enterprise Reform guidance, and replaces the three-state taxonomy with 'Joint Force Integration SAP' and 'Strategic Enabler SAP'. Neither 10 U.S.C. 119(e) nor 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) is repealed; the mechanisms survive while the vocabulary is removed from the public charter.

timeline.label: Congress prohibits moving a capability from a CAP into a SAP without notice
timeline.text: Sections 6602 and 6603 of Public Law 118-159 add a funding cutoff to 50 U.S.C. 3091a and prohibit the head of an IC element from transferring a capability from a controlled access program to a special access program, or to anything else outside the CAP, without prior notice to the intelligence and appropriations committees and congressional leadership - subject to exceptions for urgent counterintelligence and organisational restructuring.

timeline.label: Deadline passes for the SAP access population reports
timeline.text: Section 7606(c) of the FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act required each of the six officials authorised by E.O. 13526 to establish special access programs to report to nine congressional committees, including House Oversight, on how the number of personnel eligible for SAP access will be limited to the minimum required. The one-year deadline expired on this date. No such report has been publicly released.

timeline.label: Reissued ICD 906 released
timeline.text: The PDF of the reissued ICD 906 posted by ODNI carries a creation date of 19 December 2024 and states that it supersedes the ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015. It retains unacknowledged CAPs, adds the requirement that all CAPs and accesses be recorded in Scattered Castles subject only to DNI or PDDNI exemption, and confirms that neither it nor the DoD regime reaches 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action'.

carve-out.desc: How the carve-out maps onto the allegations, step by step. The central claim on this board is that recovered material is held and worked on by private defence contractors rather than by the government, and that no one outside the program can verify this. The carve-out is the documented mechanism that makes exactly that state of affairs lawful. Sequence: (1) A cognizant authority proposes a prospective SAP and includes, at item 11.d of the SAP Approval Package Checklist, a 'Contract strategy (carve-out justification if applicable)'. (2) The Director of DoD SAPCO sends an action memo to the Deputy Secretary of Defense recommending approval as an unacknowledged SAP and carve-out status - the unclassified template in DoDI 5205.11 Appendix 3 to Enclosure 6 reads, in terms, 'The Defense Security Service will be carved out from its normal industrial security oversight responsibilities.' (3) The Deputy Secretary signs. (4) By operation of 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) the Director of DCSA is relieved of NISP oversight for that program. (5) By operation of DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 2 para 2.c, three specific things stop: DCSA no longer performs SAP security inspections at the contractor location; DCSA no longer authorises the classified contractor information systems or guest systems in the contractor SAP facility; DCSA no longer runs the counterintelligence threat and incident cross-sharing for that facility. (6) Oversight passes to a Program Security Officer appointed in writing by the cognizant authority SAPCO and exercising responsibilities 'on behalf of the SAPCO' - inside the program. (7) The signed carve-out approval and the list of carved-out facilities go into the program record file under DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 7, and DoD SAPCO holds the confirmation of which facilities are carved out under Enclosure 2 para 2.k. Nothing in this chain is disputed, hypothetical or sourced to a witness. The only unknown is the content of two documents that are known by directive to exist: the carve-out approvals signed by Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries of Defense, and the facility list DoD SAPCO maintains.

usc-10-119e.desc: The hinge, stated as plainly as it can be. A witness alleging that Congress was not told about a program is usually assumed to be alleging a crime. Under 10 U.S.C. 119(e) that assumption is wrong. The Secretary of Defense may lawfully decide, case by case, that telling the defense committees something would adversely affect national security, and thereupon tell only the chairman and ranking minority member of each committee instead. There is no committee veto, no ISOO concurrence, no court, no register of waivers, no expiry, no periodic requirement to widen access, and no penalty. Compare the covert action regime, which is normally described as the most secretive corner of American government: under 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B), when access to a finding is limited to the Gang of Eight, the President must within 180 days either open it to all members of the intelligence committees or file a further written statement of reasons. A waived special access program has no such clock. That comparison is the single most useful fact this domain contributes to the board: the mechanism at the centre of the Grusch allegations is lawful, is older than the allegation, is weaker than the covert action rule it is usually compared to, and leaves an auditable paper trail in exactly two places - the Secretary's waiver determinations, and the Senior Review Group's annual review of all waived programs.

four-regime-map.desc: Where a program could sit, and what changes when it moves. There are five distinct legal environments, and the practical differences between them are the map of where concealment is easiest. (1) A DoD special access program: reports to six defense committees, waivable to eight to twelve members by the Secretary's own determination. (2) An NNSA special access program: same committees, and the Administrator may additionally waive the 30-day advance notice itself, so a program can begin with no committee ever having been told in advance - and NNSA material is Restricted Data, born classified by operation of the Atomic Energy Act rather than by an original classification authority, so a presidential declassification order operating on E.O. 13526 information does not reach it. (3) A non-DoD, non-NNSA, non-IC agency special access program: reports to House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security among others, and the waiver does not narrow the audience - the strongest of the SAP regimes, and the one covering DHS, NASA, Justice and Commerce. (4) An IC Controlled Access Program: no waiver at all, semiannual briefings, a funding cutoff since December 2024 and, since December 2024, a prohibition on transferring a capability out into a special access program without notice. (5) A National Security Council covert action program: outside all four SAP regimes by the express terms of ICD 906 section C.3, governed only by 50 U.S.C. 3093. The seam that matters is between (4) and (1). Before 23 December 2024 there was no statutory requirement to notify anyone when a capability moved from an IC controlled access program into a DoD special access program, and the move changes both the governing statute and the committees entitled to know. Congress closed that door prospectively in section 6603 of Public Law 118-159 - and left it ajar with an exception for transfers 'necessary to maintain access in the event of an organizational restructuring', a determination the transferring official makes for himself.

sap-annual-report.desc: The single most valuable unreleased document on this board. It exists. It has existed in annual editions since the first one fell due under 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1). It lists, by unclassified nickname, every DoD special access program in the budget, with a brief description, milestones, historical cost and six years of cost estimates. Its accuracy is certified before submission by the Senior Review Group and validated annually by the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. It is coordinated with the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Legislative Affairs under DoDI 5545.02. Programs whose reporting has been waived under 119(e) are, by definition, absent from it, and the substitute material given to the chairs and ranking members 'shall remain in DoD custody' with no copies stored outside DoD repositories. Three things follow for anyone trying to force the record open. First, the assertion that the government does not know how many special access programs it has is false and is contradicted by DoD's own governance directive. Second, the difference between the count in the annual report and the count on the Senior Review Group's waived list is a single number that would, if produced, tell the public how much of the SAP enterprise is invisible to the committees as a whole. Third, that number has never been requested in public by any member of Congress at any hearing this board has recorded.

sap-taxonomy.desc: Terms of art, precisely, and why each one matters to the allegations. ACKNOWLEDGED: existence admitted, details classified. If a recovery program were acknowledged, its nickname would be in the annual report and the argument would be over. UNACKNOWLEDGED: 'enhanced security measures ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized'. This is the state in which a truthful official can decline to confirm or deny, and in which a denial issued by a press office staffed by people without access is a denial made in good faith by people who genuinely do not know. WAIVED: an unacknowledged SAP whose statutory reporting has been removed by the Secretary. This is the state in which the phrase 'Congress was not informed' can be simultaneously true and lawful. Cross-cutting these are the mission categories - acquisition, intelligence, and operations and support, the last defined to protect 'the planning for, execution of, and support to especially sensitive military operations' and expressly capable of protecting 'organizations, property, operational concepts, plans, or activities'. The word 'property' in an official DoD definition is the closest thing in the public policy corpus to a category designed for custody of a physical object whose existence is itself the secret. And any SAP with subordinate structure is an 'umbrella' with 'compartments, sub-compartments, or projects' - which is why a person read into one compartment can truthfully testify to what he was told about others without ever having seen a document.

dod-sapco-arch.desc: The closed loop, drawn once. Follow the arrows and every one returns to the same office. DoD SAPCO writes the criteria for the annual review of waived programs. DoD SAPCO holds the confirmation of which contractor facilities are carved out of DCSA oversight. DoD SAPCO is the single point of congressional liaison for every DoD special access program. Everyone accessed to a DoD SAP must notify DoD SAPCO when they brief a member of Congress. No contractor may give SAP material to a member of Congress without DoD SAPCO's approval. DoD SAPCO's Director is the Executive Secretary of the SAPOC, the Vice Chair of the Senior Review Group and the Chair of the SAP Senior Working Group, and is appointed by, and reports directly to, the Deputy Secretary of Defense - the same official who signs carve-outs and to whom the Secretary's waiver authority is functionally delegated in practice. There is no external validator anywhere in the loop. That is not an allegation; it is the organisational chart set out in DoDD 5205.07, DoDI 5205.11 and DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1. The Director of DoD SAPCO has never testified in open session and the incumbent's name is not published.

accm.desc: The floor beneath the floor. Every congressional SAP reporting statute - 10 U.S.C. 119, 50 U.S.C. 2426, 50 U.S.C. 3348 - is triggered by the term 'special access program'. Alternative Compensatory Control Measures are defined in the NISPOM rule as the security measures used 'where SAP controls are not required'. An ACCM therefore is not a SAP, and no reporting statute reaches it: no annual report, no new-program notice, no 30-day report-and-wait, no waiver needed because there is nothing to waive. ACCMs carry nicknames, access rosters and compartmented handling, and 32 CFR 117.23 imposes contractor obligations for them in the same supplement as SAPs and SCI. For anyone building a picture of where an activity could be run with the least congressional visibility, ACCM is the answer that requires no waiver, no Deputy Secretary signature and no entry on any list Congress receives. The number of ACCMs in existence has never been reported to Congress because no statute requires it.

sap-cover-mechanisms.desc: What the tradecraft looks like in DoD's own words. Three documented mechanisms convert an unacknowledged program into something that leaves almost no trace in ordinary paperwork. First, nicknames: every DoD SAP gets an unclassified two-word nickname from the Joint Staff NICKA system, and it is the nickname, not the mission, that appears in the annual report to Congress. A member reading the list sees words. Second, HVSACO - HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY - which is applied when using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged program, to protect 'sensitive relationships', and to protect information that does not warrant classification at all, and which the manual states 'is not a classification'. Material marked HVSACO is therefore outside the E.O. 13526 declassification machinery entirely: it cannot be the subject of a mandatory declassification review, automatic declassification at twenty-five years, or a classification challenge, because those remedies operate only on classified national security information. Third, unacknowledged locations: DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1 provides that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations' - a rule that exists because there are facilities at which producing a federal badge would itself constitute a disclosure. Together these are the answer to the recurring question of why decades of FOIA requests have produced so little: much of the relevant paper is either inside a compartment or bears a caveat that is not a classification and therefore has no declassification pathway.

icd-906.desc: Why the intelligence side is the harder problem and the softer target at the same time. Harder: ICD 906 has no statutory annual report deadline, no 30-day pre-initiation clock and no publicly reported program list, and unacknowledged CAPs may be created on the signature of two people, the DNI or the Principal Deputy DNI. Softer: since 15 March 2022 the statute at 50 U.S.C. 3091a requires semiannual briefings on every controlled access program in effect to the intelligence and appropriations committees and congressional leadership, requires annual reports listing every active and every terminated compartment and sub-compartment with a DNI certification that each is substantiated and justified and a named control officer for each, contains no waiver authority whatsoever, and since 23 December 2024 cuts off National Intelligence Program funding for any CAP established without notification. On paper the IC has the strongest special-access oversight regime in the United States government and the DoD has the weakest. ICD 906 also does two things of direct forensic value: it requires that all CAPs and all individual accesses be recorded in Scattered Castles, the IC personnel security database, with exemptions approvable only by the DNI or PDDNI and reviewed annually - so a person's access history is a queryable record - and it expressly disclaims application to programs 'under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action', identifying the one remaining space that neither SAP regime reaches.

gao-04-332.desc: The audit that was steered. When officials say the special access program system is subject to oversight, the honest test is to ask what the Government Accountability Office has actually examined. GAO-04-332 is the only public GAO product on the security of cleared contractor facilities under the National Industrial Security Program. It was requested by the Senate in the report accompanying the FY2004 NDAA. It found that DoD could not provide adequate assurances that its oversight ensures the protection of classified information, and that DSS had not always followed required procedures after reported compromises. And its second footnote records that, 'As agreed with committee staff', the review deliberately excluded DSS's oversight of special access programs at contractor facilities. The auditor was sent into the building and asked not to open one set of doors - by agreement with the committee that commissioned the audit. Every subsequent assertion that the contractor SAP system has been independently examined has to be measured against that sentence.

gaps: The number of DoD special access programs currently designated as waived under 10 U.S.C. 119(e). This is a retrievable agency record: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 assigns the Senior Review Group an annual review of all waived DoD SAPs and requires it to ensure the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress before the annual report. The delta between the annual report count and the waived list is a single integer that has never been requested in public by any member of Congress.

The signed carve-out approvals. DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 7 requires every SAP record file to contain 'Written approval by SecDef or DepSecDef of carve-out status when DSS is relieved of industrial security oversight responsibilities' and 'The identification of SAP facilities ... that have been carved-out based upon this authority'. Neither the number of carve-outs in force, nor the list of carved-out facilities, nor the identity of any approving official for any individual carve-out has ever been published or FOIA-released.

The identity of the current Director of DoD SAPCO and the office's organisational chart, staffing and budget. DoDD 5205.07 requires the Director to be a general officer, flag officer or SES appointed by and reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. No DoD SAPCO director has ever appeared before a public congressional hearing and the incumbent's name is not published.

The DoD Manual 5205.07 Volumes 2, 3 and 4 (Personnel Security, Physical Security, Marking). As of 12 August 2026 the esd.whs.mil URLs for all four volumes do not return the documents to ordinary public retrieval; only Volume 1 was recoverable, from an Internet Archive capture dated 18 October 2019. Volume 4 (Marking) in particular would document the DoD counterpart to the CAPCO marking rules for SAP material.

The exact signature date and signer of the reissued ICD 906. The released PDF was generated on 19 December 2024 and states that it supersedes the ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015, but the signature block in the released scan is an image that does not resolve to text.

The classified addenda to the IC Authorized Classification and Control Markings Register. The public register states on its title page that 'Certain security markings were removed due to classified content. These markings have been compiled in separate classified addenda.' The existence of compartment markings that appear in no public authority is documented; their number and identity are not.

The 50 U.S.C. 3348 reports. Every federal agency other than DoD, NNSA and the IC that runs a special access program owes an annual February 1 report to congressional oversight committees expressly including the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. No such report from any agency has been publicly identified, and no public record shows House Oversight invoking this entitlement in the UAP context.

The section 7606(c) reports required by the FY2024 Intelligence Authorization Act. Each of the six officials authorised by E.O. 13526 to establish special access programs was required, by 22 December 2024, to report to nine congressional committees on the number of personnel eligible for SAP access and how it would be held to the minimum. No such report has surfaced publicly. Whether they were filed is answerable by a single letter from any of the nine committees.

Whether any waiver under 10 U.S.C. 119(e) has ever been exercised in connection with a UAP-related program, and whether the funding prohibitions of FY2024 NDAA section 1687 and FY2024 IAA section 7343 have ever been triggered, complied with, or certified against. Neither the Secretary of Defense nor the Director of National Intelligence has publicly stated whether any disclosure was made under either section.

GAO and DoD Inspector General coverage of the SAP enterprise. The only located GAO product touching contractor industrial security, GAO-04-332, expressly excluded special access programs from its scope by agreement with committee staff. No GAO product in the govinfo GAOREPORTS collection was located that audits DoD SAP congressional reporting, carve-out administration, or the waived-program list. Whether classified GAO or DoD IG products on these subjects exist, and under what report numbers, is unresolved.

The current DoD SAPCO-held count of SAP facilities (SAPFs) and of contractor SAPFs. DoDI 5205.11 requires the identification of carved-out facilities to be maintained; the total inventory of accredited SAP facilities has never been published even in aggregate.

The Prospective SAP (PSAP) register. DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 6 shows that a program can operate as a PSAP with enhanced security measures approved before it is ever approved as a SAP, on a 180-day path to a Deputy Secretary decision. Programs that were terminated as PSAPs before approval - as KONA BLUE was at DHS - never appear in any SAP report to Congress at all. No register of PSAPs initiated and terminated has ever been released.

Names of individuals holding SAPOC and Senior Review Group seats at any given date. The seats are defined by position in DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3, so the membership on any past date is reconstructible from public appointment records, but no such reconstruction exists on this board and it would identify precisely who was in the room when any given program was approved.
